entries.title: Republicans Are Running Ads Attacking 'Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed'
entries.summary: Michigan’s Democratic Senate candidate said he saw this coming.
entries.content:
Moments after Abdul El-Sayed narrowly won his Michigan Senate primary, Republicans released their first general election attack ad against him — this time, using his full name.

Ahead of El-Sayed’s November matchup against Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers, the National Republican Senatorial Committee and other GOP officials began to draw attention to the Democrat’s full name: Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed.

The NRSC had almost exclusively referred to El-Sayed, who could become the country’s first Muslim senator, by the shorter version of his name until this week. Using his full name, the committee’s debut ad slammed him as “the most radical Senate candidate in America” and connected him to the Muslim Brotherhood’s Egyptian branch, which the State Department recently classified as a terrorist group.

Other examples immediately started piling up, from the Republican National Committee casting El-Sayed by full name as a “terrorist supporter” to NRSC Vice Chair Jim Banks’ comments saying Michigan’s union Democrats wouldn’t “want to vote for a guy like Abdulrahman El-Sayed.”

Emphasizing El-Sayed’s full name and casting him as a terrorist follows a familiar strategy of using Islamophobic rhetoric to target Democrats of color: Conservatives often invoked — and, sometimes, continue to invoke — former President Barack Obama’s middle name, Hussein, as a derogatory reference despite his not being Muslim. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani encountered Islamophobic comments during and after his campaign, while former Minnesota Rep. Keith Ellison faced repeated attacks over his faith as the first Muslim to serve in Congress.

Sign up for the NOTUS Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

“That’s the only play they got. They’re gonna point at me, they’re going to point at my name, like, ‘Wow, he’s different,’” El-Sayed said in a news conference Wednesday. “You can’t actually talk about what you want to do? My name is not raising your gas prices. My name is not taking us to war. My name is not the reason you can’t afford your groceries.”

“This is the best place in the world to be Abdul,” he added.

Targeting candidates based on their Muslim faith or perceived connection to the religion is commonplace, said Dawud Walid, executive director of the Council on American-Islamic Relations’ Michigan chapter. But this behavior is rarely admonished in public, he added.

“Islamophobia is the accepted form of bigotry in American politics,” Walid said.

Republicans are framing the attacks on El-Sayed as a response to his denunciation of Israel’s actions in Gaza, a campaign issue that has loomed over many of Michigan’s elections this year The NRSC’s first general election attack ad called out his connection to left-leaning streamer Hasan Piker, with whom the Michigan Democrat has campaigned this year. El-Sayed says he supports “equal rights to peace, dignity and self-determination for Palestinians and Jewish Israelis alike.”

“And to all of my sisters and brothers of the Jewish faith or any faith or no faith at all,” El-Sayed said Wednesday, “I want you to know that my commitment to your safety — my commitment to Jewish safety — is the same commitment that I have to the safety of my own daughters.”

Beyond using his full name, many Republicans are characterizing the progressive candidate as everything from a “terrorist” to a “radical” to a “communist.” Rogers called El-Sayed an “extremist” and linked him to the Muslim Brotherhood in a statement Wednesday.

“I spent years hunting terrorists and bringing Osama Bin Laden to justice. Never in a million years did I think that I would be running against someone who believes America deserved 9/11,” misattributing Piker’s words to El-Sayed, who has never made those comments.

The NRSC did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

An RNC press release used El-Sayed’s name as wordplay, saying, “Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Is A Terrorist Sympathizer Who Wants To Take A Sledgehammer To America, Believes America Deserved 9/11, And Let Terrorists Run The Show.”

After El-Sayed was declared the winner on Wednesday, House Speaker Mike Johnson warned against communism, part of an emerging conservative talking point meant to dissuade moderates from supporting progressive candidates.

“We must take a stand and FIGHT to protect the greatest nation in the history of the world from being overrun by Mini Mamdanis,” he said on social media.

President Donald Trump, who prominently promoted “birther” conspiracies against Obama and frequently references his predecessor’s middle name, accused El-Sayed of being a “hater of Jews and Israel” as he veered into an extended riff on communism during an economic rally speech.

“Abdul El-Sayed. Can you believe this? This could only happen to me,” Trump said on Wednesday, over-enunciating the Michigan Democrats’s name to boos from the audience. “Abdul El-Sayed, lovely gentleman — he’s a man of hate."

Trump referenced El-Sayed’s full name again on Thursday, writing on Truth Social that the only thing they had in common was their desire to end the filibuster.

Michigan holds some of America’s largest Muslim and Arab-American populations — though El-Sayed’s primary win shows a wide percentage of people outside of those communities didn’t hold his religion “against him,” Walid said.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Massachusetts), who backed El-Sayed ahead of the primary, said the “name-calling” is distracting from policy issues.

“It's ugly,” Warren told reporters Wednesday. “I wish it wouldn't happen in America, but at the end of the day, I don’t think they’re going to work. I think people see through that now, and they want to hear how their candidate for Senate is going to make their lives better.”

This story has been updated to include the president’s Thursday Truth Social post.

entries.title: The Pentagon Must Resume Reviewing Wind Projects, Judge Says
entries.summary: At least 125 wind projects have been stalled because of the Department of Defense’s review freeze.
entries.content:
The Department of Defense must resume reviews of wind energy projects, a federal judge in Oregon ordered Thursday.

At least 125 utility-scale wind projects across 25 states have been stuck in limbo because of a freeze on wind project reviews at the Pentagon, according to a group of trade associations, wind energy companies and environmental organizations that sued over the delays under the Administrative Procedure Act.

The review freeze has caused a “total halt of all wind project development in the United States,” the plaintiffs said in their complaint.

U.S. District Judge Karin Immergut, a Trump appointee, said the Defense Department had violated its regulatory deadlines by withholding reviews. She issued a preliminary injunction, ordering Defense officials to provide status reports every 30 days that address whether reviews of wind projects have resumed.

Since 2011, the Pentagon has been required to conduct security reviews for new energy construction projects. The agency looks at whether those developments would have an “adverse impact to military operations and readiness.”

The review process is multifaceted. First, the Defense Department conducts a preliminary review. Then, for structures over 200 feet tall — including wind turbines — the Federal Aviation Administration gets involved, conducting an aeronautical study. For projects that could pose a risk to military operations, the Defense Department, the FAA administrator and the secretary of homeland security act as a team to identify mitigation measures — a process meant to take 90 days.

But wind projects across the country have been frozen in that process for months, as the Department of Defense gradually stopped executing those reviews last August. At first, the department stopped signing completed agreements with developers and stopped providing developers with draft agreements. In April, Defense officials cancelled negotiations with wind energy applicants who were in mitigation discussions.

In May, officials issued guidance geared toward reassessing the review process for energy projects that could cause “impactful Doppler interference,” a category that only applies to wind turbines.

Defense officials said that a freeze was necessary because of the “advancement of adversarial capabilities and the evolving global threat-picture,” citing recent drone warfare in Ukraine and Iran.

According to Dale Marks, an assistant secretary of defense, the concerns are over the potential obstruction of radar signals from a Doppler effect created by spinning turbine blades.

Lawyers for the Department of Defense asked for the case to be dismissed, arguing that concerns over national security should take precedence over the interests of energy developers. The delay in wind energy reviews has been a “practical result” of a larger reassessment of the department’s efforts to reassess its risk-assessment processes, they said in a motion to dismiss.

President Donald Trump has long publicly voiced his opposition to wind energy. His administration has attempted to stifle wind energy development at every turn, including paying out billions to companies to sever offshore wind contracts.

At a hearing Tuesday, government lawyers said that reviews for wind projects had resumed, but could not provide an example of a wind project currently moving through that process.

entries.title: McConnell Says He's Been Released From Rehabilitation Facility to Recover at Home
entries.summary: The senator’s office did not say when he would return to the Capitol after being absent for months.
entries.content:
Sen. Mitch McConnell’s office says the Kentucky Republican has been released from a rehabilitation center and will continue his recovery from home.

“Earlier today, I was discharged from the rehabilitation center to continue my recovery at home,” the senator said in a statement released by his office. “Elaine and I are grateful for the many well wishes and support from friends, colleagues, and Kentuckians, and for the attentive care I’ve received from excellent doctors, nurses, therapists, and hospital staff.”

McConnell, 84, has been absent from the Senate since his office said he fell at his home in Washington in June. The senator spent roughly four weeks in hospital care and then went to a rehabilitation center in mid-July to continue physical therapy, according to his office.

He has not been seen or heard from publicly for months, though his office has released a photo of him with his wife, Elaine Chao, from the rehabilitation center. He said in Thursday’s statement he would not be returning immediately to the Senate, which is still in session before a planned August recess.

“On the advice of my doctors, I’ll maintain an intensive regimen of physical therapy from home during the state work period, and I’ll continue to engage with my staff and colleagues on important Senate business,” he said in the statement released by his office.

The senator voted by proxy in the Agriculture Committee on Thursday, as allowed by Senate rules.

entries.title: Sen. Jon Husted Calls on Rep. Max Miller to Resign
entries.summary: Both Ohio senators have now urged the embattled congressman to step down over allegations of domestic abuse.
entries.content:
Sen. Jon Husted called on Rep. Max Miller to resign from the House on Thursday, after remaining mostly tight-lipped when asked earlier this week about the ongoing controversy involving the fellow Ohio Republican.

“Anyone who commits domestic violence is not fit to serve in Congress,” Husted wrote on X. “The House Ethics Committee should thoroughly investigate any credible allegations, and any member found to have committed domestic violence should resign from Congress immediately.”

The Ohio Republican said he is “deeply saddened” that Miller and his ex-wife Emily Moreno’s personal lives “have become such a public matter.”

“I believe Max would be making the right decision to step aside as a candidate and resign from Congress to focus on what is in the best interest of his daughter,” he wrote.

Husted’s comments follow those from Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio), Emily Moreno’s father, who on Sunday called for Miller to step down and seek professional help. Sen. Moreno told CNN on Thursday that he has moved his daughter and granddaughter “out of state to a secure place” as the controversy heightens around her ex-husband.

Earlier this week, Husted told NewsMax he wanted to let those involved “sort through this at a family level” and added that he hoped President Donald Trump would intervene to “move things along.” Husted declined to comment last week when NOTUS asked him if Miller should be replaced on the ballot in his race for Ohio’s 7th Congressional District.

When asked why it took him until now to call on Miller to resign, Husted told reporters: “That speaks for itself.”

The House Ethics Committee opened an investigation into allegations of domestic violence and illegal drug use after the congressman demanded an ethics probe into himself on Tuesday.

Emily Moreno has accused Miller of throwing scalding water on her, shoving her against a wall and holding a gun to her head. He has denied those allegations and another claim that he caused his daughter’s broken collarbone.

Despite mounting calls for him to resign, the two-term congressman has said he plans to stay in the race. Miller told CNN that House Speaker Mike Johnson is “standing behind” him — though Johnson later said things “don’t look good” for Miller in an interview with Politico.

entries.title: Mitch McConnell Is Voting, But He’s Still on Medical Leave
entries.summary: The Kentucky Republican broke ties on amendment votes “by proxy” on the farm bill Thursday.
entries.content:
Sen. Mitch McConnell wasn’t at the Agriculture Committee’s markup of the farm bill Thursday, but the Kentucky Republican was casting tie-breaking votes on partisan issues.

Yet his absence is why the bill did not advance to the Senate floor.

McConnell, who hasn’t been seen in public for almost two months while on medical leave, voted “by proxy” on each amendment presented during the meeting. Committee rules allow absent senators to authorize a senator who is present at a meeting to cast a vote in addition to his or her own. 

Chair John Boozman (R-Arkansas) said in his opening remarks that he spoke Wednesday night with McConnell, who approved his use of proxy votes as Boozman votes. “I know how much he would have wanted to be here to advocate for Kentucky's farmers and rural communities,” Boozman said.

They were McConnell's first votes since he started his medical leave, his office said.

McConnell has been on the agriculture panel from the beginning of his time in the Senate, and his proxy votes kept the bill in shape for Republicans. Democrats called for votes on numerous amendments, and all but one failed by 12-11 in favor of Republicans.

That included a Democratic-backed amendment to delay for two years when some states must start sharing costs under the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, the central issue holding Democrats back from supporting the farm bill in its current form. Republicans made the changes to SNAP in a 2025 reconciliation law.

Although some other senators voted by proxy while in and out of the meeting, McConnell was the only committee member to not appear during the meeting.

But Senate rules are different when it comes to a vote to advance the bill to the Senate floor, when proxy votes “cannot make the difference in successfully ordering a measure or matter reported to the Senate,” according to the Congressional Research Service.

Both McConnell and Sen. Tommy Tuberville (R-Alabama) voted by proxy in the final vote, so the bill was not advanced to the floor. The committee is in recess and could come back later Thursday. But the outcome won’t change unless Democrats change their votes or McConnell makes a surprise appearance.

Boozman had attempted to meet Democrats halfway on SNAP, including in the latest version of the farm bill a one-year delay for states to reduce their payment error rates below 6% to avoid sharing the cost of the program. Democrats, including Sen. Amy Klobuchar of Minnesota, the ranking member of the panel, have demanded a two-year extension.

During the markup, Klobuchar noted several times that states with the highest error rates, including Alaska, received an exception from the cost shifting to court the vote of Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) during the passage of the 2025 reconciliation law.

Boozman and Senate Majority Leader John Thune said the one-year extension is the best deal they were able to provide that still maintains support from the White House and from House leadership.

Boozman told reporters after the failed vote that he expects Democrats will go back home and hear from their constituents about the importance of passing a farm bill before trying again in September.

“They're going to be busy with their constituents in rural America, farmers and local business people. I think they're very, very disappointed that we didn't get something done,” Boozman said. “We're going to come back in that first week — have another vote on the same bill again.”

entries.title: White House Begins Head Start Program Overhaul
entries.summary: The cuts reflect a wider move to shrink education funding and regulations while shifting more authority to the states.
entries.content:
The Trump administration moved Thursday to start overhauling the Head Start program, which provides free early-childhood education and parent-support services to low-income children.

Health and Human Services officials say the proposed changes are meant to encourage more local decision-making, telling reporters on a call that “one-size-fits-all mandates cannot fully account for the realities facing” the 1,600 providers across the country.

The proposed rule would limit how much Head Start centers can spend on administrative overhead, cut federal regulations and shift control over standards like student-teacher ratios and background checks from the federal government to the states. Though the program falls under HHS, the cuts also reflect the White House’s recent moves to shrink education funding and regulations while ceding more autonomy to the states.

“Federal mandates can certainly hinder local decision-making, drive up costs and limit the program’s reach,” Alex Adams, an assistant secretary at HHS, said on the call Wednesday. “If we get this proposed rule right, we will grow the number of Head Start slots.”

Head Start enrolls nearly 716,000 children, from birth to age 5, from low-income families. Since the program’s inception under President Lyndon B. Johnson in 1965, it has served more than 40 million children and their families.

Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, whose uncle Sargent Shriver founded the program, spoke positively of the proposed changes on a preview call Wednesday.

“It’s a program that works for the most vulnerable of the poorest kids in our society, and it’s really important we protect it,” Kennedy said.

Sen. Patty Murray (D-Washington), who sits on the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee, slammed the deregulation effort.

“President Trump has all but declared war on Head Start and affordable child care in America,” Murray, a former teacher, said in a Thursday statement. “After Congress and the nation forcefully rejected Trump’s efforts to destroy Head Start, this administration now wants to quietly gut Head Start by eliminating the basic health and safety standards our kids rely on — well, I refuse to stay silent about this travesty.”

The proposal has a 60-day public comment period. Murray encouraged parents and teachers to speak out against the Trump administration's proposed erasure of regulations for the program.

“This rule is not final,” Murray said in her statement. “I will press administration officials when they come before Congress, I will sound the alarm as loudly as possible, I will carry this fight in every negotiation I walk into — and I will keep at it until we protect Head Start.”

The new proposal would toss out nearly all of the program’s regulations — which mandate research-backed curriculum and services like medical and dental screenings — forcing Head Start operators to rely on the typically more lenient state or local child care licensing requirements.

“This proposed rule would eliminate Head Start’s high standards, potentially putting the early learning, health, and safety of our youngest children at risk, and placing the future of the entire program in jeopardy,” Whitney Pesek, senior director of federal child care policy at the National Women’s Law Center, said in a statement.

entries.title: Jeanine Pirro Finds Her Limit
entries.summary: The Reflecting Pool criminal cases pit the former Fox News host’s prosecutor background against the president’s preferred path.
entries.content:
Jeanine Pirro took on the role of the top prosecutor in Washington, D.C., with two personas: a bombastic Fox News host willing to pursue politically charged issues with zeal, and a former Westchester County prosecutor and judge who wants to run a U.S. attorney's office with a sense of normalcy.

President Donald Trump's botched Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool project put those sides at odds — and her job at risk.

Pirro is now facing what so many Trump loyalists have experienced: public criticism from the president when their expertise clashes with the stance from the Oval Office.

Over the past 14 months, Pirro has had no equal in pursuing the issues most closely tied to Trump's personal spats. She launched an investigation into then-Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell, tried to indict six Democratic lawmakers, and has trumpeted arrests as part of the president's crackdown on D.C. crime that included deployment of National Guard troops.

But her office has struggled to deliver the results Trump wants. She was forced to drop the Powell probe. A grand jury declined to indict the lawmakers, part of her record that includes other failures to get indictments. There have been rebukes from federal judges about charging decisions and the abrupt dropping of charges involving alleged assaults on federal officers.

Pirro in January touted a "huge downturn in the crime statistics in just a short period of time" and said the safety of D.C. residents remains her office's top priority. Her office, in a brief statement Thursday, said there were double-digit drops in violent gun crimes, homicides and robberies in the District on her watch, reductions that “represent meaningful progress in the areas that most directly impact community safety.”

Property crime in Washington, D.C., is down so far in 2026, according to Metropolitan Police Department statistics. Yet the District has seen a sharp spike in violent physical assaults involving a dangerous weapon, and as a result, violent crime is up this year, MPD data shows.

Her 14 months in office hasn’t been enough time to assess her record for the whole office by the numbers. There are too many cases still ongoing, and Justice Department data only captures the early days of her time there. There’s another blind spot too: Her office stopped releasing monthly reports about its local cases at the start of the second Trump administration.

Pirro’s office said Thursday it has charged 68% more cases than the previous year in D.C. Superior Court.

Pirro’s relentless enforcement of Trump’s political agenda has exhausted many assistant U.S. attorneys, led to errant prosecutions, and fueled doubt among judges and jurors in Washington that her office can be trusted to bring worthy cases, several former Justice Department officials said.

“In terms of faith and public trust in the justice system, it’s causing damage that’s going to take a long time to repair, if it can be repaired at all,” said Randall Eliason, a law professor and former federal prosecutor in Washington.

“For a prosecutor, your credibility is everything,” Eliason said. “Judges are now much more willing to entertain claims of government misconduct, and that’s going to be true for juries as well.”

Pirro’s office prosecutes local violent crime through the D.C. Superior Court, the District's version of a county court. Those cases included those against alleged pool vandals and the felony indictment against a former Olympian, David Hearn.

When asked at a press conference in early July if she charged the case harshly because Trump had called for a felony charge for what he claimed was vandalism, she defended the decision. “This is a case with tremendous evidence, and this is a case where the evidence dictates where we land,” she said.

Weeks later, she filed a motion dismissing the cases and directly contradicting the president, writing that "the damage was the result of a botched installation and not vandalism.”

The filing sharply criticized the Interior Department for failing to turn over information showing the contractor, not Hearn, was responsible for the damage. Prosecutors said they had made dozens of requests before officials “slowly started trickling” the details to them. Had Interior officials been forthcoming with the information, they said, they would not have sought a grand jury indictment.

Trump nevertheless took Pirro to task, saying she had made a mistake in moving to drop the case. Pirro soon after met with Trump at the White House and could be seen carrying a white box and rolling briefcase as she crossed the grounds.

Paul Butler, a former federal prosecutor, said it was clear from the government’s court briefs that Pirro never should have charged Hearn. The evidence was so thin, he said, that prosecutors conceded in their motion to dismiss that they never could have gotten a conviction.

“She ultimately did the right thing in that case by asking the court to dismiss the prosecution,” he said. “We can imagine other prosecutors who would have died on the hill with Trump there, even if it meant getting the scorn of judges and juries.”

But Pirro’s forceful refutation of the case may have also helped her office escape deeper scrutiny — perhaps even a bar referral for bringing a case that appeared to lack probable cause, Butler said.

“The defense was threatening to petition the court for the complete grand jury proceedings and perhaps she didn't want that record exposed,” he said. “The D.C. federal bench has not been reticent in holding prosecutors accountable.”

Eliason agreed that dropping the case not only helped avoid another high-profile dismissal or acquittal, but may have helped Pirro ward off a situation where the court would have had a chance to expose potential prosecutorial misconduct before the grand jury.

That “could be not only embarrassing but could lead to professional sanctions against her and her prosecutors,” he said.

A spokesperson for Pirro declined to comment on questions related to the Reflecting Pool case, her conversations with Trump and criticisms of her office’s casework.

Pirro’s office is currently juggling several of the most high-profile criminal cases of the second Trump administration: pursuing the death penalty against the man accused of gunning down two Israeli embassy employees last year, prosecuting the man accused of trying to attack the White House Correspondents’ Association dinner this year and charging a person accused of being the failed pipe bomber who’d become the obsession of MAGA-world conspiracy theorists.

Internally, some career prosecutors who worked at the office have focused on this: At least she’s not Ed Martin.

Martin, a “Stop the Steal” MAGA activist who defended insurrectionists, laid waste to the District’s U.S. attorney’s office when he fired prosecutors who worked on Jan. 6 cases — wiping out an entire class of young prosecutors who had just undergone special training and were about to take on everyday street crime cases in D.C.

Martin also reassigned senior attorneys as punishment, demoting Jason McCullough, a veteran prosecutor who helped secure convictions against Proud Boys leaders like Enrique Tarrio. Martin lasted less than four months and lost the job when Trump couldn’t get Senate approvals.

But that meant Pirro inherited an office that was short on experienced staff — and facing a sudden wave of cases that came as a result of Trump’s decision to flood Washington with law enforcement and National Guard troops. Pirro promptly reconfigured the ranks, re-elevating experienced prosecutors like McCullough, who was once again made a supervisor. (McCullough did not respond to a NOTUS request for comment.)

“At first, there was a sense that we may not love her but she kind of understood this sort of basic prosecutorial function,” one former employee said. “She was trying to run a district attorney's office, and she'd done that before. Some people were like, ‘We don’t hate her, actually.’”

Two sources who worked in that office told NOTUS that there were two Pirros: one trying to run the office with a sense of normalcy and another willing to do the president’s bidding — to a point. A former employee said Pirro wasn’t willing to resist administration pressure the way federal prosecutor Danielle Sassoon did when she resigned last year after briefly leading the Southern District of New York.

“She wasn’t that person. … She was willing to do the White House work,” the former employee said. “Now she's looking at clear evidence from the Interior Department, and she's not going to perjure herself. She's willing to be a public advocate, but she doesn't want to perjure herself.”

Her record also reflects that, compared to the last Senate-confirmed U.S. attorney to run the office, the former Fox News host spent more energy touting her office’s efforts. During the Biden administration, U.S. Attorney Matthew Graves at the same point in his tenure filed 467 cases in federal court marked as “criminal” and touted the office’s work in 304 press releases, according to a NOTUS review of federal court dockets. Pirro has filed fewer cases (381) and issued twice as many press releases (674).

Pirro’s approach to the job also stands in sharp contrast to her predecessor in the first Trump administration, Jessie Liu, who led the U.S. attorney’s office without significant drama for more than two years and maintained the office’s independence from the White House.

“I think a lot of people, including judges, thought that she was actually pretty reasonable. She was like a typical U.S. attorney who would be appointed by a Republican president,” Butler, the former prosecutor, said of Liu, who received a unanimous Senate confirmation vote in 2017.

When Trump swore in Pirro in May 2025, he said he remembered her “as good as anybody I've seen” during her time as a district attorney. “And that was a serious prosecutor, and she went after real criminals, not fake criminals like we seem to do today, nowadays, people that shouldn't be prosecuted,” Trump said.

After Pirro’s office dismissed the Hearn case, Trump said she choked. “I was disappointed with Jeanine Pirro, really disappointed with Jeanine Pirro,” Trump said. “She, uh, she folded like an umbrella, and people get away with things, and it's a disgrace.”

entries.title: Democrats ‘Plant a Flag’ Against Hegseth’s Media Restrictions
entries.summary: A bill to restore reporter access to the Pentagon sets an early marker for the party’s oversight agenda.
entries.content:
A group of 14 Senate Democrats is set to introduce a bill Thursday to reverse Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s restrictions on media access inside the Pentagon, arguing the administration is denying the public vital information about the Iran war.

Led by Sen. Brian Schatz (D-Hawaii), the bill would restore reporters’ access to areas of the Pentagon that credentialed journalists could enter before the Trump administration’s 2025 restrictions, including the “Correspondent’s Corridor,” a workspace for journalists since 1972. The bill hasn’t previously been reported.

“Well, it's a free country, and they're not acting like it,” Schatz told NOTUS. “Especially in a time of war … a vigorous and adversarial press gets to question why we're at war, what the theory of victory is, how much it's going to cost, what our strategy is — and none of that has been explained to the public.”

The measure is unlikely to advance in the Republican-controlled Congress, and President Donald Trump could veto it if it did. But ahead of November’s midterm elections, the legislation offers an early glimpse of how Democrats could challenge one of the administration’s most contentious transparency fights if they regain power. The bill’s introduction also comes as the Pentagon is battling over the restrictions in court.

The bill’s co-sponsors include Sen. Chris Coons of Delaware, the Senate Defense Appropriations Subcommittee’s top Democrat; Sen. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee. Sens. Tim Kaine of Virginia, Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, and Jacky Rosen, all senior Senate Armed Services members, also signed on.

“Freedom of the press is enshrined in everything that we do in our democracy, and it is absolutely abhorrent to me what they're doing with limiting press access and driving out the press from the Pentagon,” Sen. Tammy Duckworth (D-Illinois), a co-sponsor and SASC member, told NOTUS. “You don't do that unless you're trying to hide something.”

Duckworth said Democrats are using the bill to “plant a flag” for future efforts to rein in what she called the administration’s “horrific attacks on our democracy.”

The legislation follows actions from Hegseth that led to the ouster of the Pentagon’s resident press corps, including requiring journalists to be escorted through much of the building, relocating major news organizations from their longtime office space and imposing new credentialing rules.

The Pentagon didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

Hegseth, who has not held a press briefing in three months, and Trump have been openly hostile to journalists reporting on national security. In the wake of a Washington Post report that he grilled Hegseth over munitions shortages during a closed-door meeting, Trump denied the shortages in a Thursday social media post and threatened that leakers of “treasonous statements are being hunted down,” and “Long term jail sentences will be sought!”

The Justice Department last month sent subpoenas to compel testimony from New York Times reporters who wrote about security concerns involving the new Air Force One before withdrawing them. In January, the FBI raided a Washington Post reporter’s home as part of an investigation into a Pentagon contractor the administration said had illegally retained classified documents.

The Pentagon policies prompted two lawsuits by The New York Times, which argued the restrictions violated the First Amendment. The administration has defended the measures as necessary to protect classified information.

A federal judge last month ordered the Defense Department to temporarily halt the requirement that journalists be accompanied by an official escort.

Schatz’s bill argues the restrictions broke with decades of bipartisan practice. If enacted, it would restore press access that existed before Hegseth initiated the restrictions, restore unescorted access for credentialed reporters, and ensure that security reviews for Pentagon credentials are conducted by career officials in the Pentagon Force Protection Agency rather than political appointees.

It would also bar future defense secretaries from changing press workspaces, access areas or credentialing rules without first consulting the House and Senate Armed Services committees.

Former CNN Pentagon correspondent Barbara Starr, now with USC Center on Communication Leadership and Policy, said the restrictions fundamentally changed how reporters can gather information in response to breaking news and made spontaneous newsgathering nearly impossible. Wartime, she said, makes open access even more important.

“Americans want to know every single day what the troops are up to, what they're being asked to do, and do they have the equipment and the training to do what they're being asked to do?” she said. “And that comes from having the press corps there on site to be able to do the reporting to answer those questions.”

entries.title: Rand Paul Takes Another Swing at Getting Fauci Federally Prosecuted
entries.summary: Republicans on the Senate Homeland Security committee voted to hold the former pandemic advisor in contempt of Congress for pleading the Fifth.
entries.content:
Republican Sen. Rand Paul is pushing the Justice Department a fourth time to investigate Anthony Fauci.

Republicans on the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, which the Kentucky senator chairs, voted Thursday to hold the nation’s former COVID-19 adviser in contempt of Congress.

Paul said he would refer the resolution to the Department of Justice rather than sending it to the full Senate, where Democrats would likely block it.

It’s unclear whether the Justice Department will take action. While Fauci remains a punching bag for Republicans furious over pandemic restrictions, the agency previously declined to investigate him under both presidents Joe Biden and Donald Trump.

In response to a question about the latest resolution, DOJ spokeswoman Kiersten Pels told NOTUS that “the department seriously reviews all congressional referrals.”

It was a testy hearing between Republicans and Democrats Thursday morning. Sen. Gary Peters, the top Democrat on the committee, attempted to stop Paul from moving forward with the vote, urging the committee to table the contempt resolution. Peters claimed Democrats on the committee were left in the dark during Paul's investigation.


"Following a one-sided investigation and a rushed process that has repeatedly excluded the minority and other members of this committee, the chairman is now asking the committee to take a vote that could harm our ability to future conduct investigations and disregards constitutional protections," Peters said.

"There has been an unprecedented access to records," Paul later retorted. "They have all been uploaded to a website you were invited to join. You refused to join. You had utter disdain. You never even asked for the password."


Ultimately, Peters' efforts failed.


The 85-year-old infectious disease expert — who became the polarizing face of the government’s pandemic response under both Trump and Biden — repeatedly invoked the Fifth Amendment to refuse to answer questions at a fiery hearing last week over his COVID-19 advice to Americans.

Democrats and Republicans on the panel were sorely divided over whether Fauci could be held in contempt for his approach.

Witnesses subpoenaed by Congress can invoke the Fifth Amendment if they’re worried about self-incrimination. Fauci was pardoned by Biden on Jan. 19, 2025, protecting him from federal prosecution for things he did or said before then.

But the pardon doesn’t protect Fauci from state prosecution — something GOP attorneys general in Louisiana, Alabama and Florida have said they’re considering. Sen. Tommy Tuberville (R-Alabama), who is running for governor, said at last week’s hearing that Fauci should be “locked up” and suggested he should be put on trial.

Fauci suggested he is fearful of prosecution, saying at the hearing’s outset that he believed Paul has an “unhinged obsession” with jailing him.

Fauci has kept a low profile in recent years, but Paul’s release last week of diaries he kept during the pandemic resparked a furious public debate over the origins of the coronavirus.

Republicans and conservatives say Fauci lied to the public about the virus’ origins, although his diary entries show he believed early in the pandemic that it came from an animal. Scientists remain divided over whether the origin was natural or from a lab leak, although more side with the possibility that it passed from an animal to a human.
